summary: Discusses ways to exchange routing information across provider boundaries when one side understands CIDR and the other does not. It also covers what running CIDR-capable inter-domain protocols such as BGP-4 means for routing inside a domain. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Two neighbors use different map styles. This memo explains how they can still share directions when only one understands the new kind of map.

subtitle: Guidance for routing information exchange during CIDR deployment

tldr.problem: As the Internet transitioned from classful to Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), some providers became capable of handling CIDR prefixes while others could not, creating a routing compatibility challenge.
tldr.mechanism: This memo categorizes providers by their routing requirements (Type 1-4) and specifies how CIDR-capable and non-capable providers should exchange routing information and aggregate routes across peering boundaries.
tldr.outcome: The guidance helped providers navigate a gradual, multi-phase transition to CIDR without requiring simultaneous upgrades of all networks. It is now Historic as the transition completed.

today: RFC 1520 is Historic. The three-phase transition it describes was completed in the mid-1990s, with the Internet's major providers adopting CIDR and BGP-4. Modern networks assume full CIDR support is universal.

sections.title: CIDR Deployment and Provider Boundaries
sections.content:
RFC 1520 addresses a critical challenge during the Internet's transition to Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR). The document defines how CIDR-capable providers (those that can forward packets based on IP prefixes rather than class A/B/C addresses) should exchange routing information with providers that cannot yet handle CIDR.

CIDR had been adopted to address the scaling crisis caused by the explosion of classful routes. However, deployment would not happen instantaneously across the entire Internet. This memo acknowledges the reality of a multi-phase rollout and provides practical guidance for the intermediate phases when networks with different capabilities must peer with each other.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet's routing system was changing. Some networks could use the new system right away, but others couldn't yet. This explains how they should work together while some are upgrading.

sections.title: Provider Types and Routing Requirements
sections.content:
The document partitions providers into four categories based on the volume of inter-domain routing information they must acquire to meet their operational needs.

Type 1 providers require a full routing table and cannot rely solely on default routes. These are the major backbone networks that must route to most of the Internet. Type 2 providers can use default routes but need a large percentage of the full routing table for optimization. Type 3 providers use default routing supplemented by a small set of explicit routes. Type 4 providers rely entirely on default routes and need no other routing information.

This taxonomy became important because the solution for each type during the CIDR transition differed significantly, particularly regarding aggregation and de-aggregation of routes.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks fall into four groups based on how much routing information they need: some need almost everything (Type 1), some need a lot (Type 2), some need just a little extra (Type 3), and some only need a default path (Type 4).

sections.title: Three-Phase Deployment Plan
sections.content:
The memo assumes CIDR deployment would proceed in three phases. In phase 1, all Type 1 providers would deploy BGP-4 and transition to CIDR. This included the major backbone networks that form the Internet's core. Upon completion of phase 1, CIDR reachability information would begin appearing in the Internet.

In phase 2, Type 2 providers connected to the phase-1 providers would transition, along with some Type 3 providers. This phase would bring significant routing simplification by shifting aggregation responsibility to providers better equipped to handle it.

In phase 3, the remaining Type 3 and most Type 4 providers would transition. The document anticipated each phase lasting progressively longer, with phase 1 being shortest and phase 3 being the longest.
sections.plainLanguage: The upgrade would happen in three waves: first the biggest networks, then medium networks, then smaller networks and simple ones.

sections.title: Exchanging Information Across Boundaries
sections.content:
The core contribution is guidance for each peering scenario. When a CIDR-capable provider exchanges routes with a Type 2 (non-CIDR) provider, the CIDR provider can aggregate routes it receives (compress many specific routes into one broader route) only when the Type 2 provider requests it. The Type 2 provider receives either explicit classful (non-CIDR) routes or a default route, plus any CIDR routes if the CIDR provider chooses to explicitly split them back out.

When peering with Type 3 providers, the exchange is similar: aggregation is receiver-driven (the CIDR provider aggregates on request only), and Type 3 providers typically use default routes plus a few explicit routes to reach destinations covered by CIDR information.

For Type 4 providers, which need only a default route, the exchange is simplest: a CIDR-capable provider sends a single default route.

All exchanges should be controlled by bilateral agreements between directly connected providers, specifying which types of information can be exchanged, aggregated, or de-aggregated. Making these agreements accessible (for example in a policy database) helps with troubleshooting.
sections.plainLanguage: When a new-style network talks to an old-style network, they agree on what information to share. The new-style network can bundle together routes if the old-style network asks for fewer, more general routes.

sections.title: Interior Routing and CIDR Capability
sections.content:
A CIDR-capable provider has two main options for distributing exterior (inter-domain) routing information internally. The first is to run internal BGP or IDRP between all routers, treating the interior of the domain as a single autonomous system. This requires no special changes to the interior routing protocol.

The second option is to use a CIDR-capable interior routing protocol (such as OSPF or IS-IS with CIDR support) and inject exterior routes into it. This reduces reliance on internal BGP but imposes requirements on the interior routing protocol and requires routers to support injection of inter-domain routes into intra-domain routing.

Crucially, all routers within a CIDR-capable provider must themselves be capable of CIDR-based forwarding; the compatibility requirement extends throughout the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks using CIDR need to pick how they'll share big routing tables inside themselves. They can either run their version of BGP on all routers, or teach their internal routing to understand the new addressing.
